title: Image Quality and Failure Subgroup Analysis
main_findings: Good-quality cases generally showed the strongest performance across the frozen pipeline, including higher segmentation overlap, lower quantitative errors, and higher EF-band classification accuracy.
Median ED Dice decreased from 0.9519 in Good-quality cases to 0.9439 in Medium and 0.9130 in Poor cases.
Image-quality effects were not uniform across ED and ES. Medium-quality cases showed the largest median ES area error and ESV error, whereas Poor-quality cases showed the lowest median ED Dice.
Median segmentation-induced EF error was 3.6443 pp for Good, 4.6977 pp for Medium, and 9.0898 pp for Poor-quality cases.

Median end-to-end EF error was 5.2637 pp for Good, 8.2648 pp for Medium, and 7.6206 pp for Poor-quality cases. Therefore, downstream degradation was not strictly monotonic with the ordinal quality labels.
EF-band classification accuracy was 80.0% in Good, 53.85% in Medium, and 57.14% in Poor-quality cases.
Classifier confidence, confidence margin, and entropy were similar across image-quality groups, indicating that classifier confidence did not clearly reflect CAMUS image-quality category.

Among the exploratory Kruskal-Wallis comparisons, ESV absolute error showed the clearest subgroup difference (H = 7.9553, p = 0.0187). However, multiple outcomes were examined and the Poor-quality subgroup contained only seven patients, so this result is not treated as confirmatory evidence.
interpretation: CAMUS image quality is associated descriptively with performance degradation in parts of the frozen pipeline, but its effect is stage-specific rather than uniformly monotonic. Good-quality images generally perform better, while Medium and Poor cases show different error patterns across ED/ES segmentation, quantitative measurements, and classification. Image quality therefore provides useful context for robustness analysis but cannot by itself serve as a complete patient-level reliability indicator.
application_implication: Image-quality information may be useful as one component of a future quality-control or review mechanism. The present results do not justify rejecting or accepting an analysis solely from the CAMUS Good/Medium/Poor category.
limitations: The Poor-quality subgroup contained only seven patients.
Subgroup analyses were exploratory and multiple outcomes were examined.
No pairwise post-hoc significance testing was used to select findings.
CAMUS ImageQuality is existing dataset metadata and is not an independently validated automatic quality score from the current system.
The evaluation set had historical pilot exposure.
